newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN DEBT SPRITELY AS WAGES STIRS RATE IDEAS.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN DEBT SPRITELY AS WAGES STIRS RATE IDEAS.

text.p: *The Australian debt market put in a more spritely performance as thoughts once again turned to the possibility of another rate cut after benign final second quarter wages data.
*U.S. Treasuries face July CPI later on Thursday.

The Australian debt market saw its strongest performance for some weeks as thoughts once again turned to the possibility of another easing in monetary policy after the release of a benign set of final wages data.
At one stage during an active session December bill futures contract was practically pricing in a 25 basis point easing in current 5.0 percent official rates at a contract high of 95.23.
"We believe that over the next few months the market will move to price a 4.5 percent cash rate into the yield curve," said John Peters, senior economist at Westpac Banking Corp.

Peters, and other economists, expect the Reserve Bank to endorse the move with a 50 basis point rate cut in late October/early November and after the next round of inflation and average weekly ordinary time earnings data.

Overall final wages growth was revised down to 0.3 percent in the second quarter, bringing the annual rate to 3.5 percent from a preliminary 3.7 percent, while key private sector wages surprisingly fell 0.1 percent for an annual rate of 2.5 percent.
"Whichever way you look at the data, wage growth has slowed, reducing inflationary pressures," said Craig James, senior economist at Colonial State Bank.

"Where does that leave the much-awaited strengthening in activity? Employment growth is flat, existing employees are getting only modest wage increases and are concerned about their jobs. That leaves confidence - the achilles heel of the economy," he added.
Indeed, the August Westpac consumer confidence survey released on Wednesday rose only 0.2 percent, which was seen as a fairly disappointing response to the July official rate cut.
The long end of the curve also responded to the wages outcome, which helped to extend a shortcovering rally which started late yesterday and put aside its recent U.S. worries.
The September 10-year bond futures contract cut through several resistance levels to touch a high of 93.380, a solid bounce from Wednesday's 93.135 low.
However, the market still has some way to go to get back to the all time high of 93.695 set on August 1.

Meanwhile, U.S. Treasuries were firm in Tokyo trading ahead of the July CPI later on Thursday. The U.S. market had failed to hold onto all of its strong gains in New York on Wednesday which were made in the aftermath of the July PPI falling for a seventh consecutive month and the 0.6 percent rise in retail sales being below the 1.0 percent-plus the market had feared.

The local rally saw the market put in a strong outperformance against the dollar bloc. The Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread was heading back towards last week's 25 basis point low after nearing 50 basis points on Wednesday.
